question: Does the law expect the officer who first registers a case to be the same one who investigates it, or are those meant to be separate roles — and does that match what actually happens in our data?
expected_answer: The law expects separation. Article 18 of the Police Order, 2002 sets up a distinct Investigation Wing under a dedicated head of investigation, states that registered cases "shall be investigated by the investigation staff" under that head, and bars the District Police Officer from interfering in the investigation process — the clear intent is that logging a case and investigating it are separate functions. In practice, our data shows the opposite: the officer who records the FIR and the officer who ends up investigating it are the same person in 68 of 74 pairs (92%); role-splitting happens in only 6 cases. So the separation the law sets up isn't what's actually happening on the ground in this data.
actual_answer:
### Governing Provision:
The law does not explicitly require the officer who first registers a case to be the same one who investigates it. According to [Document 4], a police officer may investigate a non-cognizable case only with the order of a Magistrate, and any police officer receiving such an order may exercise the same powers in respect of the investigation (except the power to arrest without warrant) as an officer in charge of a police station may exercise in a cognizable case. This implies that the officer who registers the case (often the one who receives the information) may not necessarily be the same as the one who conducts the investigation, especially in non-cognizable cases. Additionally, [Document 7] states that an officer in charge of a station may be deputed to investigate, and in such cases, the investigation may be taken up and completed by the officer in charge of the police station or an assistant sub-inspector at the first opportunity, which further supports the idea that the roles may be separate.

### Case Records:
In our case records, the two roles (the officer who recorded the FIR and the officer who investigated it) are mostly NOT separated: the officer who recorded the FIR and the officer who investigated it are the same person in 68 of 74 recorded assignment pairs (92%). Roles are split in only 6 pair(s), across 6 case(s). Of those 6, 3 of them carry an investigating officer with no recording officer on the same case at all, so the pair is unresolvable rather than genuinely split. The remaining 3 cases have different officers for recording and investigating. This indicates that while the law allows for the roles to be separate, in practice, they are often combined.
